projects.title: Project 1: A childhood, with a stranger - crit, 5 November
projects.description:
Introduction

The Project 1 crit took place on Thursday. Wanning and I presented Childhood with a Stranger: two strangers play rock-paper-scissors via webcam, and with each round, they receive a page of a childhood story. I’d rehearsed my lines twice that morning, but still ended up forgetting half of them, so this post isn’t about what I’d originally intended to say. Instead, it’s about what the audience saw, what Boyd said, and what I’ll be incorporating into the next version.


The rules of the room

Boyd ran the crit as a Liz Lerman Critical Response Process and spent the first ten minutes explaining a single word: observation. He held up a green cup and had us describe it repeatedly until the screen was filled with descriptions: green, metallic, cylindrical, made of two parts, with a dent in the base, keeps drinks warm, probably quite expensive. He then asked everyone to make value judgements: it’s ugly, it’s beautiful, I like your website. ‘A value is our emotion.’ The first round of feedback could consist solely of observations. The artist then posed questions to the entire audience, and only after the artist had said, ‘I would like your opinions,’ was anyone permitted to express what they liked or disliked. The key point is that the artist controls what they hear. I’d read about this approach before the website crit, but it was only after witnessing the process demonstrated with the cup that I truly took it on board.

I based my explanation closely on the content of the slides: Why childhood (life moves too fast; no one ever stops to look back on the past), why ‘Rock, Paper, Scissors’ (everyone has played it; there are no rules, no words are needed, and it takes just a second), why both hands (a camera can recognise 21 feature points, yet will never be able to recognise a face), why silhouettes (shadows reveal movement, not the person, so that person could be you), why books turn into sand (just as memories fade away). Two students played a round; when we turned to the page that read ‘moms have to wear dresses’, the whole room burst out laughing.

Finally, I concluded with an apology: ‘We changed direction last week, so we didn’t have time to tell any more stories.’ Boyd interrupted me: ‘Never tell us more information than we need to know. You’ve done some really wonderful work. Let us give you feedback about what we experienced, and avoid trying to make excuses, because maybe there’s no excuses to be made.’ That was the sharpest moment of the day, and a fair one at that. That excuse told the whole room what to focus on, which ran completely counter to the original purpose of the observation session.


What the room observed

The first player said that at first she didn’t know how to play, but the pace was just right for this theme: slow, rather than fast. Someone asked whether the second partner always heard the same story. That is indeed an issue: four rounds, twelve pages, and the content of the pages is fixed. A classmate remarked that the boy’s voice sounded like an adult’s; indeed it did, because it was my voice.


Boyd’s perspective

There are three points, all of which point in the same direction.

Firstly, there is specificity. He asked whether these stories stemmed from our own childhoods. Indeed they do: mulberry trees, power cuts, removal lorries—these are all experiences that Wanning and I have lived through ourselves. He said this is precisely why these stories are so moving: ‘what becomes exciting is when the artist shares something very deep and specific about themselves, and that gives us an opportunity to identify with you.’ We had worried that these stories might be too personal to have universal appeal. He turned that perception on its head. Do not let a work of art become vague; make it concrete and vivid, so that people can recognise themselves in it.

Secondly, regarding the next version. At the end of the game, ask each player to contribute a childhood memory, just a sentence or two, to build a database. The page will grow with every playthrough. Have them record that sentence as well, so their voices become the voice of that boy or girl. And AI-generated stories must not be used; he’d already told me this in an email: real memories bring ‘a special feeling of intimacy’ that generated stories simply cannot achieve.

Thirdly, the question I hadn’t anticipated was: why a boy and a girl? I answered honestly that the first story was our own, and that boys might be more inclined to play with girls.

He asked why. I was at a loss for words. He said that this pairing presupposes a certain relationship; if the two children were chosen at random, two boys or two girls, the work would resonate with a wider audience. Moreover, the page where the boy refuses to wear a skirt is not only amusing: it also evokes memories of my own childhood, when I was told what ‘boys shouldn’t do’. The work could leave room for this, rather than merely re-enacting that experience.


My current thoughts

I had originally assumed this crit would centre on the code: whether the hand tracking was stable, and whether the sand flowed smoothly. But nobody mentioned the code. All the important discussions centred on ‘whose memory is this’ and ‘who is permitted to access it’. This is exactly what Boyd told me during our one-to-one conversation on Tuesday: anyone can implement it now; the real value lies in the concept. The concept was approved. What wasn’t approved, however, was the fact that this concept was limited to just the two of us. A memory bank, the players’ own voices, and random children would transform a story about Wanning and me into a game that others could also help create. That is the version I want to make, and this is the first time I’ve left a crit with a clear direction rather than a long list of bugs.

There’s one more thing I need to remember: next time, when the slides end, stop speaking.


References
[1] Boyd, Project 1 crit, ARTD6232, 5 November 2026 (my own recording).
[2] Lerman, L. and Borstel, J. (2003) Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process. Dance Exchange.
[3] Boyd, email reply on Project 1 routes, 28 October 2026 (no AI-generated content).
[4] Boyd, personal-tutor conversation, 3 November 2026.

projects.title: Project 0: Invisible Costs - a disposable vape (final)
projects.description:
Live site: https://af3333hy.github.io/invisible-costs-vape/
Code: https://github.com/af3333Hy/invisible-costs-vape

Introduction
Invisible Costs is a web page about a disposable vape, an object I use every day. Vapes are banned in China; in the UK you can buy them everywhere, even after the ban of June 2025. The page asks: why is it so cheap? Because other people pay: the workers who dig the cobalt, my own body, and the environment where 8.2 million vapes are thrown away every week.

Related work
All my research is on this page: the mood board (14 image sources, A to F) and the nine desk-research sources (three peer-reviewed papers, three news reports, one government page, one industry press release and one Mintel report) are the entries below this one, each with a link. Every fact on the site links to its source. For the look I followed Picasso's bull from week two (only a few lines), Todd McLellan's Things Come Apart and the pixel work of eBoy.

Method
Four pages in one HTML file. HTML is the skeleton, CSS does the look and the movement (black and white, sprite sheets with steps(), a transition for the falling vape, filter: invert for the flash), JavaScript does the actions (open a page, count the puffs, draw the mood line on a canvas, ask the model) and JSON only holds the data. All 17 key frames were drawn by me in Piskel. The "Ask the model" buttons send a fact to Ollama (gemma3) running on my laptop. The code follows Boyd's template; where I needed something not taught yet I asked AI, then rebuilt it on the template so I can explain every part.

Results
Page 1, Start: six frames of a person, one line each, from ten cigarettes a day to "I can't give it up". Page 2, Inside: click a part, it moves apart and a card shows one fact, its source and a photo of the real part. Page 3, Use: press the button to puff; the page flashes, smoke rises, the mood line sinks lower each time; after three vapes the pile catches fire, the only colour on the site. Page 4, Thirty years: one press is five years; three miners keep digging, my face goes calm, tired, then gone; at the end a company boss and a nurse answer the same fact. Shown at the crit on 15 October; live on GitHub Pages.

Conclusion
The biggest change came from Boyd's feedback on the first version: no visual centre. So I made four pages where only one thing is big, and the person, not the vape, became the main character. I now know what HTML, CSS, JavaScript and JSON each do, which words are fixed and which names are mine. My full explanation of the code, and which commits had AI help, is in my Week 4 blog (Creative Tech 1 → Blog → Week 4) and in the README of the code repository. Next: the model only runs on my laptop, so the online version needs a server; and the same person comes back in Project 1.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 1 of 9 (Peer-reviewed)
projects.description:
Reid, H. et al. (2023) 'Up in smoke: Considerations for lithium-ion batteries in disposable e-cigarettes', Joule.

This paper is about the lithium-ion battery inside disposable e-cigarettes. The researchers (2023) tested the batteries and found that they can be recharged: after more than 700 charging cycles they still kept over 90% of their capacity. I will use this number in the battery part of my page, to show that a battery made to be used once could be used hundreds of times.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 2 of 9 (Peer-reviewed)
projects.description:
Turner, A., Scott, J.W., Backshall-Kennedy, T. and Dabrowski, M.C. (2024) 'Deconstructing contemporary disposable vapes: A material and elemental analysis', Science of the Total Environment.

This paper is about what a disposable vape is made of. The researchers (2024) took apart nine types of disposable vapes. One vape weighs about 50 grams, plastic can be up to about 80% of it, and they found toxic metals such as lead, mercury and cobalt in the battery and the circuit board. I will use the plastic number for the shell and the toxic metals for the circuit board.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 3 of 9 (Peer-reviewed)
projects.description:
Iturralde, K., Karunarathne, S., Selby, P. and Zawertailo, L. (2026) 'A review of the environmental impacts of post-consumer electronic cigarette waste and disposal', Nicotine & Tobacco Research.

This review is about what happens to the environment after e-cigarettes are thrown away. It looked at 18 papers published between 2004 and June 2024. It says e-cigarettes are both hazardous waste and electronic waste, and the e-liquid harms animals and plants living in water and on land. I will use this in the e-liquid part of my page.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 4 of 9 (News / interview)
projects.description:
Kemp, O., Warnes, S. and Thomson, Q. (2025) 'UK to ban sale of disposable vapes in response to soaring waste and safety risks', CNN, 31 May.

This news article is about the UK ban on the sale of disposable vapes. It reports a Material Focus figure from 2024: about 8.2 million vapes were thrown away every week in the UK, which is 13 every second. A 17-year-old student said it felt wasteful to throw away the battery with the vape after only three days. I will use the 2024 number at the start of my page to show how big the problem is, and the student's words as the voice of a user.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 5 of 9 (News / interview)
projects.description:
Standaert, M. (2020) 'Business vapourised: Could coronavirus hurt e-cigarette makers?', Al Jazeera, 26 February.

This news report is about the e-cigarette factories in Shajing, a district of Shenzhen in China. The reporter talked to a factory boss there. The article (2020) says about 85.7% of the world's vaping devices are made in this area, and about 500,000 people worked directly in the factories in and around Shenzhen at the end of 2019. I will use this for the 'where it is made' part of my page, to show the workers behind the object.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 6 of 9 (News / interview)
projects.description:
Renewable Energy Magazine (2026) 'Lithium-ion batteries inside discarded vapes are creating thousands of battery fires across the UK', 28 September.

This article is about the battery fires caused by vapes that are thrown away, even after the ban. A survey from December 2025 to January 2026 found that 6.3 million vapes and pods were still thrown away every week (8.2 million in 2024), and 47% of vapers did not know that vapes can be recycled. More than 1,200 battery fires in one year (2023 to 2024) were linked to these batteries. I will use the fire number in the battery part, to show what happens after the vape goes in the bin.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 7 of 9 (Government)
projects.description:
Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (2025) 'Single-use vapes banned from 1 June 2025', GOV.UK, 31 May.

This is the government announcement of the ban. From 1 June 2025 the UK banned the sale of single-use vapes. It also says recycling them is slow and expensive, because each one has to be taken apart by hand. I will use the date of the ban, and the point about taking them apart by hand, in the last part of my page about what happens at the end.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 8 of 9 (Commercial / industry)
projects.description:
Material Focus (2023) 'Disposable single-use vapes thrown away have quadrupled to 5 million per week', 8 September.

This press release is about how fast the number of thrown-away vapes grew: from 1.3 million a week to nearly 5 million a week in 2023. It says the lithium inside the vapes bought in one year could power nearly 5,000 electric cars. I will use this comparison in the battery part of my page.

projects.title: Project 0: Desk Research - Source 9 of 9 (Mintel)
projects.description:
Mintel (2025) 'UK Disposable Vape Ban', Mintel Observation, 20 June. (Accessed through the University of Southampton Library.)

This Mintel observation (2025) is about how UK consumers see the disposable vape ban. 66% of UK consumers think carefully about how their daily choices affect their lifestyle. Mintel says disposable vapes were once seen as a safer choice than smoking, but they have become a big environmental and health problem in the UK. I will use this for the user part of my page, to show how people's view of the vape has changed.
